items.prompt: What is 'strategic ambiguity,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Speaking truthfully but incompletely, without creating a false impression about what you did say
Refusing to answer any question you find inconvenient
Using vague corporate language so nobody can hold you to specifics
Telling different people different versions of the same story
items.explanation: Strategic ambiguity is specifically about truthful incompleteness — what's said is accurate, just not the full picture, and the listener isn't left believing something false.
items.reference:
Strategic ambiguity
✅ True, incomplete
✅ No false belief created
❌ Not the same as refusing to engage
Why: the test is whether it creates a false belief, not whether it's vague.

items.prompt: Priya tells Sam 'I can't get into specifics about org plans right now.' Which best describes this statement?
choices: Strategic ambiguity — true and incomplete, without manufacturing a false belief
An affirmative falsehood, since it avoids the real answer
Selective disclosure that crosses into dishonesty
A lie by omission, since Sam doesn't get the full picture
items.explanation: This statement is accurate and leaves Sam correctly aware that something is being withheld — it doesn't plant a false belief, which is what would make it dishonest.
items.reference:
Strategic ambiguity
✅ True, incomplete
✅ No false belief created
❌ Not the same as refusing to engage
Why: the test is whether it creates a false belief, not whether it's vague.

items.prompt: What is 'selective disclosure'?
choices: Choosing what true information to share and what to withhold, based on authorization, timing, or relevance
Sharing information only with people you personally favor
Disclosing information exclusively through official channels
Withholding information out of pure self-interest, regardless of authorization
items.explanation: Selective disclosure is the mechanism gray politics runs on — deciding what true information to share and when, which is not inherently dishonest on its own.
items.reference:
Selective disclosure
📋 Choosing what to share, and when
🔑 Based on authorization, timing, relevance
⚖️ Neutral mechanism, not automatically wrong
Why: the mechanism itself is neutral — what matters is whether it's used to inform or to mislead.

items.prompt: Is selective disclosure, on its own, inherently dishonest?
choices: No — it's the neutral mechanism that both honest ambiguity and dishonest deception are built from
Yes — withholding any true information is always a form of lying
No, but only if the person asking never finds out
Yes, unless the person withholding has a formal legal exemption
items.explanation: Selective disclosure is neutral — it's the same underlying mechanism (choosing what to share) that both strategic ambiguity and affirmative falsehood are built from; what happens on top of it is what determines honesty.
items.reference:
Selective disclosure
📋 Choosing what to share, and when
🔑 Based on authorization, timing, relevance
⚖️ Neutral mechanism, not automatically wrong
Why: the mechanism itself is neutral — what matters is whether it's used to inform or to mislead.

items.prompt: What is an 'affirmative falsehood'?
choices: Actively stating something untrue, or something you don't believe to be true, to steer someone's belief
Any statement made with confidence, even if accurate
Declining to answer a question because you're not authorized to
A true statement delivered too late to be useful
items.explanation: An affirmative falsehood is the bright line: actively asserting something untrue to steer someone's belief, as opposed to withholding a true fact you're not free to share.
items.reference:
Affirmative falsehood
🚫 Actively stating something untrue
🎯 Meant to steer belief
🔴 The bright line into dishonesty
Why: this is the one category that's never a gray zone — it's a direct lie.

items.prompt: Priya tells Sam 'Yes, totally safe, don't worry about it.' What is this?
choices: An affirmative falsehood — Priya actively manufactured a false belief
Strategic ambiguity — a truthful, incomplete answer
Selective disclosure that stays within the honest zone
A neutral non-answer with no real content
items.explanation: This statement doesn't merely withhold information — it actively asserts something Priya knows to be false, which is exactly what defines an affirmative falsehood.
items.reference:
Affirmative falsehood
🚫 Actively stating something untrue
🎯 Meant to steer belief
🔴 The bright line into dishonesty
Why: this is the one category that's never a gray zone — it's a direct lie.

items.prompt: What is 'timing information,' as a distinct lever from truthfulness?
choices: Deciding when to disclose something true, independent of whether it's disclosed at all
Choosing the most dramatic moment to reveal information for effect
Sharing information faster than colleagues to seem more informed
Delaying an announcement until it's legally required
items.explanation: Timing information is about the 'when,' separate from the 'whether' — the same true fact can be responsible or harmful depending on how long it's held back.
items.reference:
Timing information
🕐 When to disclose, not just whether
📈 Same fact, different harm by timing
Why: truthfulness and timing are separate axes — a statement can be honest yet still poorly timed.

items.prompt: Two people share the exact same true fact, one immediately and one weeks late. What does this illustrate?
choices: Timing information — the same honest fact can be responsible in one case and harmful in the other
That truthfulness alone always guarantees a good outcome regardless of timing
That the earlier disclosure was actually dishonest for being premature
Nothing meaningful — timing has no bearing on honesty or its effects
items.explanation: This is exactly the point of timing information: identical truthful content can land very differently depending on when it's shared, independent of whether either version was a lie.
items.reference:
Timing information
🕐 When to disclose, not just whether
📈 Same fact, different harm by timing
Why: truthfulness and timing are separate axes — a statement can be honest yet still poorly timed.

items.prompt: Of Priya's two possible answers ('I can't get into specifics...' vs. 'Yes, totally safe'), which one is honest?
choices: The first — it's true and incomplete, without asserting anything false
The second — it's more reassuring and reduces Sam's anxiety
Both are equally honest, since neither reveals the reorg
Neither is honest, since both withhold the reorg from Sam
items.explanation: The first answer is truthful and leaves Sam correctly aware something is unsaid; the second actively asserts a false 'yes,' which is what makes it dishonest, not the fact that both keep the secret.
items.reference:
Priya's two answers
🗣️ "Can't get into specifics" — honest
🗣️ "Totally safe" — dishonest
Why: both keep the secret; only one of them lies about what's true.

items.prompt: Both of Priya's candidate answers keep the reorg secret. What separates the honest one from the dishonest one?
choices: Whether the answer creates a false belief, not whether it keeps the secret
How much detail is included in each answer
Whether Sam ends up feeling reassured afterward
Whether the answer is delivered kindly or bluntly
items.explanation: Both answers protect the confidential reorg information equally — the distinguishing factor is whether the answer manufactures a false belief in Sam's mind, which only the second one does.
items.reference:
Priya's two answers
🗣️ "Can't get into specifics" — honest
🗣️ "Totally safe" — dishonest
Why: both keep the secret; only one of them lies about what's true.

items.prompt: Is leaving someone with an incomplete picture automatically dishonest?
choices: No — most workplace conversations involve leaving things out for confidentiality, relevance, or brevity
Yes — any omission is a form of lying by default
Only if the person withholding is in a position of authority
Only if the topic is about compensation or job security
items.explanation: Incompleteness alone isn't the problem — nearly every conversation omits something; what matters is whether the omission is paired with a manufactured false belief.
items.reference:
Withholding ≠ dishonest
✂️ Incomplete is normal
🚫 False belief is the actual problem
Why: confusing incompleteness with dishonesty misses the actual test.

items.prompt: What actually makes withholding information cross into dishonesty?
choices: When it's paired with actively creating a false belief, not merely an incomplete one
When the information withheld is about something important
When more than one person is kept in the dark at once
When the withholding lasts longer than a single conversation
items.explanation: Withholding by itself is common and often necessary — it becomes dishonest specifically when it's combined with actively manufacturing a false belief rather than an honest 'I can't say.'
items.reference:
Withholding ≠ dishonest
✂️ Incomplete is normal
🚫 False belief is the actual problem
Why: confusing incompleteness with dishonesty misses the actual test.

items.prompt: What is the single test that separates honest ambiguity from dishonesty, according to this unit?
choices: Whether the statement creates a false belief, not whether it's vague or incomplete
Whether the speaker feels guilty about what they said
Whether the listener eventually finds out the full truth
Whether the statement was legally required to be made
items.explanation: The unit's core test throughout is the false-belief test: vagueness and incompleteness are fine on their own; what crosses the line is actively creating a false belief.
items.reference:
The core test
❓ Does this create a false belief?
✅ No → ambiguity is fine
🚫 Yes → dishonest territory
Why: this single question resolves nearly every case in the unit.

items.prompt: Why doesn't waiting until you need to disclose something to figure out how to phrase it work well?
choices: Because by the time the question lands, you need a clear line already in mind, not one improvised under pressure
Because repeating a vague phrase is enough as long as it is technically true
Because the safest line is always the shortest possible answer
Because the listener's inference is never part of the speaker's responsibility
items.explanation: Having the false-belief test clear in advance is what lets someone give a genuinely honest answer under pressure, rather than reaching for reassurance in the moment.
items.reference:
The core test
❓ Does this create a false belief?
✅ No → ambiguity is fine
🚫 Yes → dishonest territory
Why: this single question resolves nearly every case in the unit.

items.prompt: According to the withholding-vs-lying comparison, what does the listener walk away with in each case?
choices: Withholding leaves 'I don't have the full picture yet'; lying leaves a specific false belief they'll act on
Both leave the listener with the exact same impression
Withholding leaves a false belief; lying leaves an incomplete picture
Neither leaves the listener with any usable impression
items.explanation: The comparison table's key distinction: withholding leaves the listener aware they don't have everything, while lying leaves them with a specific, actionable, false belief.
items.reference:
Withholding"I don't have the full picture"
LyingA specific false belief acted on
Why: the listener's resulting mental state is the real comparison point.

items.prompt: Which is more reversible if it comes out later — withholding or lying?
choices: Withholding — 'I wasn't free to say more' generally holds up; a discovered lie does not
Lying — being caught lying is generally seen as more forgivable than withholding
Both are equally reversible once the full truth comes out
Neither is ever reversible once discovered
items.explanation: The comparison table shows withholding as reversible when explained honestly later, while a discovered lie reads as a deliberate betrayal that's much harder to walk back.
items.reference:
Withholding"I don't have the full picture"
LyingA specific false belief acted on
Why: the listener's resulting mental state is the real comparison point.

items.prompt: If Priya's strategic-ambiguity answer comes out later as having been about the reorg, what typically happens to trust?
choices: It generally holds up — 'I wasn't free to say more' is usually understood as normal discretion
It's treated exactly the same as if she had lied outright
Trust is destroyed regardless of what she actually said
It only holds up if Sam never asked a direct question in the first place
items.explanation: Because the original statement was true, explaining the constraint afterward ('I wasn't free to say more') generally repairs any friction — this is the reversibility that a discovered lie doesn't have.
items.reference:
Reversibility
✅ Withholding: explainable later, holds up
🚫 Lying: discovered as deliberate, doesn't
Why: the difference isn't just how it feels in the moment — it's whether it survives being explained afterward.

items.prompt: If Priya's 'totally safe' answer comes out later as having been false, what typically happens to trust?
choices: It reads as a deliberate betrayal, since a specific false statement was made on purpose
It repairs just as easily as an honest ambiguous answer would
Nothing changes, since the reorg outcome was outside Priya's control
Trust actually improves, since Sam was spared anxiety in the meantime
items.explanation: An affirmative falsehood, once discovered, reads as intentional deception rather than discretion — there's no equivalent to 'I wasn't free to say more' that repairs a statement that was actively false.
items.reference:
Reversibility
✅ Withholding: explainable later, holds up
🚫 Lying: discovered as deliberate, doesn't
Why: the difference isn't just how it feels in the moment — it's whether it survives being explained afterward.

items.prompt: In the decision flowchart, if you can't share the full truth and your answer won't leave the listener believing anything false, what's the verdict?

Flowchart branches

⚠️ False belief, unstated → gray zone

Flowchart branches
✅ No false belief → ambiguity, fine

items.prompt: Why is timing described as a 'separate axis' from truthfulness?

Because timing determines whether a statement counts as true at all
Because true statements can never be mistimed
Because timing only matters for statements that are already lies
items.explanation: Truthfulness asks whether what's said is accurate; timing asks whether it's shared (or revisited) at the point where it's actually needed — they're independent questions.
items.reference:
Two independent axes
✅ Truthful — is it accurate?
🕐 Timely — is it shared when it matters?
Why: a statement can score well on one axis and poorly on the other.

items.prompt: Two colleagues each share the same true fact — one right away, one weeks late. Both statements are equally truthful. What can still differ between them?

Nothing — if both are equally truthful, the outcomes must be identical
Whether either one counts as an affirmative falsehood
Whether either one counts as strategic ambiguity at all
items.explanation: Equal truthfulness doesn't guarantee equal outcomes — the delayed version can cause real harm precisely because timing is a separate, independent factor from accuracy.
items.reference:
Two independent axes
✅ Truthful — is it accurate?
🕐 Timely — is it shared when it matters?
Why: a statement can score well on one axis and poorly on the other.
